title: “Trust, not features, is the real deficit”: VMware tries to appease SMBs
gist: Broadcom is planning an updated, lower-priced vSphere Standard edition after admitting its sales team over-pushed the costly VMware Cloud Foundation bundle onto small businesses, but partners and analysts say three years of aggressive VCF-only tactics have already driven many SMBs to rivals like Nutanix, Proxmox, and Microsoft Hyper-V.

themes.theme: Broadcom's pricing pushed SMBs away from VMware

insights.claim: Broadcom's acquisition of VMware ended perpetual license sales and introduced expensive, stacked subscription bundles that priced many small-to-medium businesses out of the product.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Identifies the licensing shift as the root cause of SMB attrition, directly relevant to Broadcom's addressable market in the segment.
insights.locator: Broadcom's acquisition of the virtualization firm

insights.claim: VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), Broadcom's flagship private cloud bundle, has been criticized by SMB customers as unaffordable and stuffed with unnecessary offerings, and some sales representatives falsely claimed the lower-priced vSphere Standard edition was no longer available.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Documents a specific sales practice that eroded customer trust beyond just pricing, complicating any attempt to win SMBs back.
insights.locator: Many SMBs find that VCF is unaffordable

insights.claim: VCF chief product officer Paul Turner admitted Broadcom's sales incentives had encouraged the sales team to push VCF too aggressively and said the company has now 'corrected' that focus.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A rare on-record admission from VMware leadership that its own sales incentive structure caused the SMB pricing backlash.
insights.locator: Speaking with The Register this week, Paul Turner

themes.theme: vSphere Standard neglect and planned update

insights.claim: VMware has not updated vSphere Standard since 2022, despite VCF 9 receiving an updated version of vSphere in 2025, because the company prioritized improving VCF's security instead.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Quantifies the multi-year product neglect that gave competitors an opening to court disaffected SMB customers.
insights.locator: VMware hasn't updated vSphere Standard since 2022

insights.claim: Broadcom's Infrastructure Software Group president Ram Velaga said VMware avoided introducing a lower-end virtualization product because customers 'could get distracted' from the push toward private clouds as a cheaper alternative to public cloud.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Reveals the deliberate strategic reasoning behind sidelining the entry-level product, not just an oversight.
insights.locator: Velaga said that VMware prioritized VCF

insights.claim: VMware will release an updated version of vSphere Standard 'soon,' with more details expected in October at VMware's Explore conference in Frankfurt.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete near-term catalyst investors and partners can watch for signs of a genuine SMB-focused pricing reset.
insights.locator: VMware will release an "updated version" of vSphere Standard

insights.claim: Dean Colpitts, CTO of Canadian managed services provider Members IT Group—cut from VMware's reseller program after 19 years—said his company is doing no VMware business now and won't in the future because Broadcom 'burned all the bridges.'
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A concrete example of a long-tenured channel partner permanently exiting the VMware ecosystem, illustrating lost channel revenue.
insights.quote: Broadcom has burned all the bridges. While it may be easier to migrate to whatever this new [vSphere] Standard release is from vSphere 8, they have already shown both customers and [channel] partners they can't be trusted,
insights.locator: Dean Colpitts, CTO of Canadian managed services provider

insights.claim: Sumit Bhatia, co-author of a book on the Broadcom-VMware transition, said three years of neglect and VCF-only sales tactics have already pushed many SMBs toward Nutanix, Proxmox, and Microsoft Hyper-V, arguing 'trust, not features, is the real deficit.'
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Names the specific competitors capturing displaced VMware SMB customers, useful for tracking competitive share shifts in virtualization.
insights.quote: Trust, not features, is the real deficit. Broadcom must prove sustained commitment—stable pricing, reliable renewals, and real investment—before SMBs treat vSphere Standard as safe again.
insights.locator: "An updated vSphere Standard signals Broadcom heard the market

insights.claim: Bhatia said a credible vSphere Standard relaunch would need predictable published pricing with no surprise renewal spikes, a genuine capped-term or perpetual-style license option, and core features like vMotion and High Availability without upsell gates.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete checklist investors and customers can use to judge whether Broadcom's upcoming release is a genuine fix or cosmetic.
insights.locator: A vSphere Standard update would need

insights.claim: Broadcom's software business made $8.75 billion in revenue in fiscal Q3 2026, a 29 percent year-over-year increase, indicating the overall business has thrived despite SMB defections.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Suggests Broadcom's software segment growth is not dependent on SMB retention, which may explain why SMB-focused fixes have been slow to arrive.
insights.locator: The conglomerate's software business has thrived
